title: Seeing Williams and Walker, conductor Vaughan and Will Marion Cook
summary: At about six or seven he sees the Williams and Walker show; the pit conductor James Vaughan makes him want to conduct, and he recalls Will Marion Cook's group.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Now, well, where I got my inspiration was, when we went to this theater, we saw Williams and Walker. Williams Bert Williams was a great comedian, George Walker was a dancer, and George's wife was also a dancer and a singer.
But the thing that puzzled me mostly, was the man in the

pit. There was a fellow named James Vaughan, I think his name was. Well, he was conductor of this orchestra. Now, so I can tell you, that's what I wanted to do. And I worked a long -- it took me forty years to get to that place, where I conducted something. But I eventually got there.

Now, it was really a treat for me, at my age, to have seen Bert Williams do his slide, his funny slides, and tell his jokes. And George Walker, who was the greatest of the strutters. He could strut better than anybody. In fact, the strut, I think the black people took from the horses. Not the race horses, the show horses. And I think the way they'd raise their legs and throw it, just like you see a race horse, a show horse, not a race horse. But, Ada Walker was a very clever singer.

Well, these things impressed me. And then, there was another man in that show called Will Marion Cook. Will Marion Cook had a group, and they did the different songs, I think was one was Exaltation, and then all of these fellows'd meet and another song, that's stayed with me a long time, because the words are, 'Brother, should smote on the right cheek, turn the other one around.' And, you know, 'there's not going to be any rain if you hear the dog barking', and things like that.
